conservation.notes: Not threatened, though the species has been studied as a model for the effects of habitat fragmentation. Some populations have been lost to toxic contamination, notably heavy-metal smelter byproducts in Idaho's Silver Valley, and to the piscicide rotenone, which killed 100% of tadpoles exposed to it before they developed lungs while barely affecting adults.

human_tolerance.notes: The species needs permanent water whose level rises seasonally and an abundant cover of low-growing or emergent vegetation, and it has been studied as a model for the effects of habitat fragmentation. A farm pond or ditch at the edge of a lot would suit it; a tilled yard would not.

phases.name: breeding
phases.note: The northeastern Oregon study observed breeding from March at the warmest low-elevation sites (922 m) through June at the highest sites (2,220 m). The Burns locale is within this regional elevation span; March-June is retained as a regional window, not a site-specific date estimate.

phases.name: young
phases.note: Egg masses of up to 1,300 eggs are laid free-floating in shallow water and hatch into tadpoles, which reach around 79 mm before metamorphosing.

inat.skipped: ISO 3166-2 region given without --inat-place-id; pass --inat-place-id <id> (look it up at https://www.inaturalist.org/places) to query iNaturalist for this subdivision

vocalizations.description: The male's chorus, which 'ranges from a series of clicks to long, glottal sounds', used to attract females to the breeding ground. Mapped to the schema's Croak context, the closest enum value to an amphibian advertisement call.

taxonomy.note: GBIF's match returns Rana luteiventris Thompson, 1913 as ACCEPTED; the article's title and lead use the same name and authorship. Order Anura and family Ranidae follow the article, which places the species among the frogs and describes it as 'closer' to the northern leopard frog than to other ranids.

external.note: gbif_usage_key is the ACCEPTED key from the GBIF species match for Rana luteiventris; inat_taxon_id is the iNaturalist taxon returned by the API match. Optional keys (ITIS TSN, Wikidata Q-number) were not looked up, so they are omitted rather than guessed.

conservation.note: 'Although not threatened, this animal has been studied as a model species for the effects of habitat fragmentation' gives the category basis, and the conservation section's toxicant findings - 100% tadpole mortality from rotenone before lung development, and disrupted reproduction from heavy-metal mixtures in the Silver Valley - are quoted from it. The article does not itself print an IUCN category word, so the LC entry rests on its 'not threatened' statement; a reviewer wanting the formal citation should check IUCN directly.

range.note: Worth a reviewer's attention: 'The Columbia spotted frog is widespread throughout western North America, from Alaska and parts of British Columbia to Washington, Idaho, and parts of Wyoming, Nevada, and Utah.' US and CA are native on the strength of that sentence, and elevation_m follows the highest elevation the article names for breeding, 2,377 m in Wyoming, with 0 as the sea-level end implied by the British Columbia February breeding date. Note that the article's range sentence does not itself name Oregon, even though its external links include Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife material on this species; the US-OR activity curve attached to this record, drawn from iNaturalist place 10 and the GBIF GADM area USA.38_1, is the record's evidence that the species occurs in the state. koppen is omitted: the article describes elevation bands and aquatic habitat but gives no climate classification.

traits.mass_kg.note: Honest gap: the article gives a maximum length of 89 mm and a tadpole length of 79 mm but no mass, and none was found on Wikidata or GBIF for this item. 0.03 kg is an authored estimate for a medium ranid frog of that snout-vent length, flagged so a reviewer can replace it with a measured mass. It is used only to set size_class and to scale the block mesh.

traits.length_m.note: The article gives 'lengths of up to 3.5 in (89 mm)' - a maximum, not a range. 0.089 m is that maximum, recorded as given and flagged by the fact that it is an upper bound rather than a typical value; no midpoint can be computed from a single figure.

traits.lifespan_y.note: The report gives oldest observed male and female ages of 9.7 and 8.7 years by skeletochronology, not typical wild lifespan. The required field is set to a 5-year authored model estimate; it is not a measured mean or maximum.

traits.diet.note: The northeastern Oregon field study reports adult diet as varied mollusks and arthropods, with beetles, ants, wasps, and flies composing more than 50% of food items. The record has no fish diet evidence. The 95/5 split is an authored simulation allocation that gives most of the diet to observed invertebrate prey; the study does not report these exact fractions or a mass-based diet composition.

traits.social.note: 'Males present a chorus to the females to try to attract a mate', and 'The male frog arrives at the breeding grounds before the female becomes reproductively active and establishes an oviposition site'. A chorus is an aggregation, so Group is recorded; the female then lays at the site the male has already established. group_size bounds are authored, since the article gives no counts.

traits.activity_pattern.note: The northeastern Oregon report describes frogs active at breeding sites in spring and summer, with males calling mostly at night and occasionally during the day; it also records calling during diurnal hours at some study sites. Cathemeral represents activity across day and night without prescribing a fixed diel schedule.

traits.defense.note: 'These frogs are a constant victim to predation', and the predator list is long at every stage, with adults taken by herons, coyotes, common ravens, American badgers, river otters and weasels. Freeze is recorded: a small, ground-coloured frog facing a large predator's shadow goes still, which is also what the shared anuran program does by freezing before it hops.

traits.nest_type.note: 'The egg masses, once laid, absorb water and become the size of a softball. These eggs are not attached to any type of vegetation, but are left free-floating in a permanent water source.' No nest, cavity, burrow or platform is prepared, so None is the matching enum value; the eggs are simply suspended in water.

traits.perching.note: The animal is aquatic or shoreline: it is 'known as a very aquatic amphibian', 'spend[s] most of their time in the water', and uses 'low-growing or emergent vegetation' as shelter rather than perching on it. False.

traits.note: Grouped entries. body_plan Vertebrate, limb_count 4, thermoregulation Ectotherm, skin Moist, respiration Lungs are the standard anuran values the article's description of a frog and its tadpoles implies. flight None follows the absence of any flying or gliding stage. metamorphosis Complete follows the article's own account of eggs hatching into tadpoles that 'reach around 3.1 inches (79 mm) in length before maturing to adults'. size_class Tiny is derived from mass_kg (under 0.05 kg), which rests on the authored mass estimate flagged above. locomotion_modes Walk, Hop and Swim: the animal moves over shore vegetation and shallow water, hops, and swims.

traits.wariness.note: Judgement set high: 'These frogs are a constant victim to predation', 'a constant victim' being the article's own phrase, with a predator list covering birds, mammals, reptiles and fish, and the species requiring dense emergent vegetation as cover because of it. flight_distance_m 5 m is short because a fleeing frog's best option is the water it is already in.

habitat.use.note: Authored from the habitat and description sections: the species is 'known as a very aquatic amphibian' that spends 'most of their time in the water' in 'permanent bodies of water, which can include lakes, ponds, slow-moving streams, and marshes', with a minority of time on shore and in emergent vegetation. Aquatic use therefore dominates.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: 'Their habitats are found generally near permanent bodies of water', and adults 'inhabit mostly seasonally flooded sites, where the water source is constant'. pond is the matching ResourceTag; the dependence is absolute, since the eggs are 'left free-floating in a permanent water source' and reproduce in the same body of water in which the frog lives.

habitat.resources.note: invertebrate 0.85 follows traits.diet. water 1.0 reflects absolute dependence on permanent water for reproduction and for most of the animal's time. shrub_thicket 0.5 is a deliberately partial entry: the article says the frogs 'require an abundant source of low-growing or emergent vegetation as shelter', which is emergent cover in and beside water rather than a woody thicket, and 0.5 keeps it below the food and water weights because the vegetation is shelter they can leave, not a resource they live in.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: Avoider and uses_gardens false follow the species' habitat requirements - permanent water whose level rises seasonally, plus abundant emergent vegetation - and the article's framing of it as 'a model species for the effects of habitat fragmentation'. The notes field records that a farm pond or ditch at a lot's edge would suit it, so a reviewer can see the distinction is about water rather than about people. light_max 0.2 and flight_distance_m 5 m are authored judgements for a small prey animal that hides in emergent vegetation.

seasonal.strategy.note: The article describes no dormancy, hibernation or migration for this frog: it is active in the water through the year and breeds in the same permanent water source in which it lives. ActiveYearRound is recorded. It is worth noting against the alternative that a high-desert locale is cold in winter - a reviewer with a sourced overwintering record for this species should add it.

seasonal.phases.note: The primary northeastern Oregon study observed breeding from March at 922 m to June at 2,220 m. The locale centroid is 1,264 m, so the full regional window is used because the study does not provide a Burns-specific date. The former February-June range came from unrelated locations and was too broad for this regional claim.

seasonal.life_stages.note: Honest gap: the article gives the egg count ('up to 1300 eggs'), the egg mass size and the tadpole length ('around 3.1 inches (79 mm)'), but no incubation period, no time to metamorphosis and no juvenile period. All three durations are authored judgements for a ranid frog, flagged rather than quoted; the Egg and Tadpole values are roughly in the range of the common toad record already in this repository, adjusted for a smaller animal. The scales are authored. The Tadpole stage is used because metamorphosis is Complete and the article describes a free-swimming larval form.

vocalizations.click_chorus.note: The report describes weak, sporadic male calling, mostly at night with occasional daytime calls, and elsewhere notes calls normally heard during diurnal hours. The FSM uses this single call only within the documented March-June northeastern Oregon breeding window; day/night timing is left open.

look.note: Colours from the description section: 'It is green to brown in color with spots on the dorsal surface. The belly and upper lip are white in color', 'Its color ranges from a dark, olive green to light brown with irregularly shaped black spots on its back and legs (rendering its name)', and 'the ventral sides of the frog are usually colored either pink or yellow, but only in the adult form'. The palette maps olive to body, white to belly, the black spots to markings and a warm tan to accent; the dorsal_spotting extra part carries the irregular black spots the species is named for, and the lip_stripe extra part carries the diagnostic 'light-colored strip ... along the upper lip'. The anuran body plan is used because that is the mesh the repository draws for frogs, and leg_length_ratio is set below the common toad's because the article notes this frog has 'shorter hind legs' than similar-sized ranids. Proportions are otherwise authored.

behavior.note: Species-local FSM based on the field report: highly aquatic adults use permanent-water breeding sites, male calls occur mostly at night but can occur by day, and adults are active across seasons. The program removes the shared nocturnal hide/rest gate and permits activity in either daylight period. Temperature and movement distances are authored simulation settings; the call gate explicitly covers March through June as reported for breeding calls.

activity.US-OR.note: GBIF-only US-OR curve regenerated 2026-10-10. The CC BY-NC tier was needed because CC0/CC BY samples did not meet the 300-record minimum; it is retained as a last-resort regional activity source.
